at.step: Top-down: split the range at its midpoint, sort each half by the identical rule, then merge what comes back — the recursion tree already named for its own recurrence, a merge at every node instead of nothing.

Bottom-up reaches the identical sorted order with no recursion and no call stack at all: merge every adjacent pair of width-one runs, then every adjacent pair of width-two runs, doubling the width until one run is left.

At a power-of-two size, every split both strategies make lands exactly in half, so their comparison counts match exactly. Off a power of two, top-down's recursive midpoint and bottom-up's fixed doubling can split some of the smaller merges differently — and the counts can differ.

The buffer, three ways: the simple version copies the whole input range on every merge; the usual refinement copies only the left half, since the right half and the output can share the original array's own space; Timsort's own refinement copies only whichever run is shorter, which can be smaller still.

Natural merge sort does not split blindly: it finds the runs an input already has — maximal ascending stretches — in one linear pass, and merges adjacent runs pairwise until one remains. Already-sorted input is one single run, and nothing is ever merged at all.

Five shapes, five very different run counts: a random input has close to half as many runs as it has keys; sorted input has exactly one; reversed input has exactly as many runs as keys, the worst case for a detector that only looks for ascending stretches.

items.item: A linked-list merge needing no buffer and an O(1) splice (named in one frame, Chapter 2) is not a contradiction of this topic's own 'merge sort needs a buffer' claim — the buffer requirement is specific to the array representation, where elements cannot be relinked in place the way list nodes can.

The merge's own min(m, n)-to-(m+n-1) comparison bound holds for any two sorted ranges, not only equal-length ones; this topic's own examples both use equal-length (eight and eight) ranges for a clean side-by-side comparison, which is a presentational choice, not a limit of the bound itself.

at.step: The merge procedure: two pointers, one per sorted range, one comparison each step, the smaller key copied out and its own pointer advanced. A perfect interleaving of the identical two ranges costs one less than their combined length — the most a merge can ever cost.

items.item: Bottom-up merge sort's own fixed-width sweep still needs to know where each width's own runs start and end, which for an array is just arithmetic on the loop index — no explicit bookkeeping structure is needed, unlike a scenario where runs have genuinely irregular, data-dependent boundaries (natural merge sort, later in this same topic).

items.item: The three real systems cited (Python, Java, Rust) are evidence for the stability-and-buffer claims this topic makes, not evidence that merge sort by itself is what any of them ship — all three are Timsort-family hybrids with run detection this topic's own natural merge sort only approximates, a distinction FACT-CHECK.md's own Red team states explicitly rather than leaving implied.

The gap between merge sort's own worst case and the information-theoretic bound being 'only' linear in n is still an absolute gap that grows without limit as n grows — 'linear growth' is not the same claim as 'the gap stays small,' and this topic's own ratio-based framing (under 0.53n) is the precise form of the claim, not a loose paraphrase of it.
